::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🎯 Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

-   Explain what deconvolution estimates, and what it cannot estimate
-   ⚠️ Say why the reference dataset determines the answer, and what to check before trusting one
-   Say why single-cell-resolution data is annotated rather than deconvolved, and where those labels go wrong
-   Distinguish a cell-type map from a **niche** map, and say why the second is where the biology usually is
-   ⚠️ Test co-localisation against a null that respects tissue structure
-   ⚠️ Say why neighbouring spots inflate significance, and what to do about it
-   ⚠️ Compare niches between patient groups with the patient, not the spot, as the unit
-   ⚠️ Say what a distance limit adds to ligand–receptor inference, and what it still cannot show
-   Place any claim on the evidence ladder from description to demonstration
-   Design a spatial validation step for a hypothesis generated in W5–W6
:::

> 🤔 **Motivating question**
>
> You deconvolve 4,000 spots and find that regulatory T cells and exhausted CD8 T cells co-occur (*p* \< 10⁻¹²). How much does that p-value tell you?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Deconvolution 🧩 {#w8-s1}

## 1) The problem, restated {#w8-s1-1}

From 🔗 [W7 §3](w7_spatial_basics.qmd#w7-s3): a Visium spot is a **mixture**. Deconvolution asks what mixture of cell types best explains the observed profile — using single-cell data as the dictionary of what each cell type looks like.

![](/assets/img/w8/deconvolution.svg){fig-align="center"}

| Method | Approach | Notes |
|----------------------|--------------------|------------------------------|
| **RCTD** | Statistical, models platform effects | robust, widely used |
| **cell2location** | Bayesian, estimates absolute abundance | ✅ gives cell numbers, not only proportions |
| **CARD** | Uses spatial correlation between spots | borrows information from neighbours |
| **SPOTlight** | NMF-based | fast |
| **Tangram** | Maps single cells onto space | useful when you have matched data |

💡 Method choice matters less than reference choice. Benchmarks separate these methods by modest margins; a wrong reference changes the answer entirely.

## 2) ⚠️ Reference bias {#w8-s1-2}

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## The failure mode with no error message

Deconvolution returns proportions that **sum to one over the cell types you supplied**. It has no way to report "there is something here I have never seen".

-   ⚠️ **A cell type absent from the reference** does not appear as missing. Its signal is redistributed onto whichever reference type is closest. This is the single-cell version of reference bias, one layer down
-   ⚠️ **A reference from healthy tissue** applied to tumour, or from PBMCs applied to tissue-resident cells, biases every proportion at once — not just the affected type
-   ⚠️ **A reference from a different platform** (Smart-seq vs 10x, cells vs nuclei) carries systematic differences into the estimates

✅ What to actually check:

-   Same tissue, same condition, ideally the **same patients** as the spatial sections
-   Verify with a marker gene you did **not** deconvolve — plot raw *CD3E* and see whether it lands where the T-cell proportions did
-   Ask whether a rare-but-important population is in the reference at all
:::

## 3) What proportions can and cannot tell you {#w8-s1-3}

-   ✅ "This region is enriched for macrophage signal relative to that region" — solid
-   ✅ "Macrophage proportion correlates with distance from the invasion front" — solid, and interesting
-   ⚠️ "This spot contains 2.3 macrophages" — only cell2location-style methods attempt absolute numbers, and with wide uncertainty
-   ❌ "These particular macrophages express gene X" — you cannot get cell-type-specific expression out of a mixture without much stronger assumptions

## 4) Single-cell resolution: annotate, don't deconvolve {#w8-s1-4}

![](/assets/img/w8/cell_annotation.svg){fig-align="center"}

On Xenium, CosMx or Visium HD the unit is a segmented cell (🔗 [W7 §3.2](w7_spatial_basics.qmd#w7-s3-2)), not a mixture. The task becomes **annotation**: one label per cell, from the same single-cell reference.

-   **Label transfer** (Seurat anchors, as in §2.3) or **RCTD in `doublet` mode** (each cell or 8 µm bin = one or two types)
-   ⚠️ **Only the panel's genes are used.** The reference has ~20,000 genes, the panel a few hundred to 5,000. A cell type with no marker on the panel cannot be called — it is forced into its nearest neighbour
-   ✅ **Map the confidence.** Low-confidence calls piling up at cell–cell contacts = segmentation spillover, not a new "hybrid" state

💡 Panel design is decided before sequencing: check that every cell type you care about has markers on the panel.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. From Cell Types to Niches 🏘️ {#w8-s2}

## 1) The question that spatial data is actually for {#w8-s2-1}

A per-spot cell-type map is useful, and it is still one location at a time. The step that uses the geometry is asking what each location is **surrounded by**.

![The interface exists only as a mixture of several cell types. No single spot defines it.](/assets/img/w8/niches.svg){fig-align="center"}

**How it works:** for each spot, build a vector of the cell-type composition of its neighbours (within *k* spots or a fixed radius), then cluster those vectors. The clusters are **niches** — recurrent tissue microenvironments.

-   Not the same as the spatially aware domains of 🔗 [W7 §4.4](w7_spatial_basics.qmd#w7-s4-4): domains smooth the neighbours' *expression*, niches cluster the neighbours' *composition*

💡 Notice what the left panel hides. T cells and macrophages are present almost everywhere and **dominate almost nowhere**, so a "dominant cell type" map erases them entirely. The immune biology is invisible until you look at composition rather than identity.

## 2) ⚠️ Testing co-localisation honestly {#w8-s2-2}

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Against which null?

"Cell type A and cell type B co-occur more than expected" requires a definition of *expected*.

-   ❌ **Complete spatial randomness** is the wrong null. Tissue is not random — it has layers, vessels, capsules, glands. Almost any two cell types will beat this null
-   ✅ **Permute labels within the tissue**, preserving the overall architecture and each cell type's total abundance
-   ✅ Or compare against **matched control tissue** — the same anatomy, different disease state

⚠️ And back to the motivating question: *p* \< 10⁻¹² across 4,000 spots is mostly telling you that you had 4,000 spots. Neighbouring spots are positively correlated by construction (🔗 [W7 §4.3](w7_spatial_basics.qmd#w7-s4-3)), so the effective sample size is far smaller than the nominal one.

→ ✅ The number that matters is the **effect size**, replicated across **patients**.
:::

## 3) Mapping single cells into space {#w8-s2-3}

The reverse direction: take a cluster you found in scRNA-seq and ask where it sits.

-   **Tangram**, **Seurat anchor transfer** — project single-cell labels onto spatial data
-   ✅ Genuinely useful for testing a specific hypothesis: *"the exhausted CD8 state we found — is it inside the tumour or at the margin?"*
-   ⚠️ Circularity risk: if the mapping uses the same genes that defined the cluster, finding the cluster is not independent evidence

## 4) ⚠️ Comparing niches between patients {#w8-s2-4}

![One large section can produce a tiny p on its own — it simply has that many spots/cells.](/assets/img/w8/patient_level.svg){fig-align="center"}

"TAM-rich niches are more common in non-responders" is a claim about **patients**, so the patient is the unit — the same logic as pseudobulk (🔗 [W5 §5.3](../part3/w5_scrna_qc.qmd#w5-s5-3)).

-   ① Define niches on **all sections together**, so a niche label means the same thing in every patient
-   ② Per patient: the **fraction of the section in each niche** → one row per patient
-   ③ Compare groups on those rows, n = patients. Fractions are compositional (🔗 [W5 §5.4](../part3/w5_scrna_qc.qmd#w5-s5-4)) → `propeller`-style tests, or a model with the patient as the unit
-   ⚠️ **Pooled spots** (a χ² on 5,000 spots) = W5's per-cell test in a new costume. One big section can carry the whole result
-   ⚠️ Several sections per patient → average them, or model the patient as a random effect. Never count them as extra patients
-   ✅ Report the **effect size with an interval**, and show one dot per patient

## 5) ⚠️ Ligand–receptor, now with distance {#w8-s2-5}

![Distance removes pairs that could never meet. It proves none of the rest.](/assets/img/w8/spatial_ccc.svg){fig-align="center"}

W6's cell–cell communication (🔗 [W6 §3.2](../part3/w6_scrna_dynamics.qmd#w6-s3-2)) scores every sender cluster against every receiver cluster — including cells that were never in the same place. Spatial data adds the missing constraint.

-   **Distance limit** — score only sender–receiver pairs within signalling range. Contact signals: direct neighbours. Secreted signals: further, up to a few hundred µm
-   `COMMOT` — optimal transport with a distance limit; ligands and receptors compete for each other
-   `CellChat` v2 — spatial mode, with separate ranges for contact and secreted signals
-   `LIANA+` — local scores: where in the section are ligand and receptor high together?
-   ✅ **Test against a structure-preserving null** (§2.2) — e.g. shift the receiver layer as a whole. Being near matters only if it is nearer than the tissue predicts
-   ⚠️ Still mRNA next to mRNA: no protein, no binding, no response. A W6 hypothesis moves to rung ③ at most (🔗 [§3](#w8-s3))
-   ⚠️ On Visium, sender and receiver can share one spot → "near" is set by 55 µm, not by biology. Single-cell platforms give the cleaner version — with the segmentation caveat of §1.4

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. ⚠️ Where This Sits in the Evidence 🪜 {#w8-s3}

![](/assets/img/w8/evidence_ladder.svg){fig-align="center"}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What spatial validation does and does not buy you

Spatial data moves a claim from **② hypothesis** to **③ consistent with**. That is a genuine, meaningful promotion — and it is not proof.

-   ✅ It rules out the most common failure of ligand–receptor inference: cells that were never in the same place
-   ✅ It gives you a figure a clinician and a pathologist can both read
-   ❌ It does not show the protein was made (rung ④), and it does not show causation (rung ⑤)

💡 For a resident's project, ③ is often the honest and achievable ceiling — and it is publishable when stated as ③. What sinks papers is writing ⑤'s verb over ③'s evidence.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Designing a Spatial Study 📋 {#w8-s4}

You now have enough to design one. The order matters.

**① Start from a hypothesis, not from a platform.** "We will do spatial on some tumours" is not a design. "We will test whether TAM-rich niches exclude CD8 T cells in non-responders" is.

**② Decide what resolution the hypothesis needs** (🔗 [W7 §2.3](w7_spatial_basics.qmd#w7-s2-3)). If the answer is "are these two cell types touching", spot-based data will not settle it no matter how you analyse it.

**③ Count patients, not sections.**

| Design | Effective n | Verdict |
|--------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------|
| 3 sections, 1 patient | 1 | ❌ a case report with 4,000 spots |
| 1 section each, 6 patients | 6 | ⚠️ a pilot; report it as one |
| 1 section each, 20 patients selected by outcome | 20 | ✅ a study |

**④ Select by outcome where you can.** Responders vs non-responders from the archive is a stronger design than consecutive consenting patients, and FFPE makes it possible (🔗 [W7 §2.2](w7_spatial_basics.qmd#w7-s2-2)).

**⑤ Secure a matched single-cell reference** before you commit — from the same tissue and condition, or budget for generating one.

**⑥ Book the pathologist first.** Block selection is a scientific decision, and it is made once.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Hands-On 💻 {#w8-s5}

## 1) Deconvolve, then check the reference {#w8-s5-1}

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(Seurat); library(spacexr); library(tidyverse)   # spacexr = RCTD

sp  <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "7_visium.rds"))
ref <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "5_pbmc_annotated.rds"))   # ⚠️ is this the right reference?

reference <- Reference(GetAssayData(ref, "counts"), factor(ref$cell_type))
puck      <- SpatialRNA(GetTissueCoordinates(sp), GetAssayData(sp, "counts"))

rctd <- create.RCTD(puck, reference, max_cores = 4) |> run.RCTD(doublet_mode = "full")
props <- normalize_weights(rctd@results$weights)
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, scanpy as sc, squidpy as sq
import tangram as tg                                    # pip install tangram-sc

sp  = sc.read_h5ad("analysis/7_visium.h5ad")
ref = sc.read_h5ad("analysis/5_pbmc_annotated.h5ad")    # ⚠️ is this the right reference?

tg.pp_adatas(ref, sp)                                   # shared genes only
ad_map = tg.map_cells_to_space(ref, sp, mode="clusters", cluster_label="cell_type")
tg.project_cell_annotations(ad_map, sp, annotation="cell_type")
props = sp.obsm["tangram_ct_pred"]
props = props.div(props.sum(axis=1), axis=0)            # per-spot proportions
```
:::


:::

⚠️ **Before believing any of it**, ask what a PBMC reference implies for a tissue section. Tissue-resident macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelium are not in it — where did their signal go?

## 2) ✅ The verification that should be reflexive {#w8-s5-2}

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Plot a raw marker gene next to the estimated proportion of its cell type
p1 <- SpatialFeaturePlot(sp, features = "CD3E") + ggtitle("raw CD3E")
sp$Tcell_prop <- props[, "CD8 T"]
p2 <- SpatialFeaturePlot(sp, features = "Tcell_prop") + ggtitle("estimated CD8 T")
p1 | p2
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
# Plot a raw marker gene next to the estimated proportion of its cell type
sp.obs["Tcell_prop"] = props["CD8 T"]
sq.pl.spatial_scatter(sp, color=["CD3E", "Tcell_prop"], title=["raw CD3E", "estimated CD8 T"])
```
:::


:::

💡 If these two maps disagree, the deconvolution is telling you about your reference, not about the tissue.

## 3) Niches {#w8-s5-3}

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(FNN)

coords <- GetTissueCoordinates(sp)
nn     <- get.knn(as.matrix(coords), k = 6)$nn.index

# neighbourhood composition per spot
nbr_comp <- t(apply(nn, 1, \(idx) colMeans(props[idx, , drop = FALSE])))

set.seed(1)
sp$niche <- factor(kmeans(nbr_comp, centers = 5)$cluster)
SpatialDimPlot(sp, group.by = "niche")
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

coords = sp.obsm["spatial"]
nn = NearestNeighbors().fit(coords).kneighbors(coords, n_neighbors=7, return_distance=False)[:, 1:]   # drop self

# neighbourhood composition per spot
nbr_comp = props.to_numpy()[nn].mean(axis=1)

sp.obs["niche"] = KMeans(n_clusters=5, n_init=10, random_state=1).fit_predict(nbr_comp).astype(str)
sq.pl.spatial_scatter(sp, color="niche")
```
:::


:::

## 4) ✅ Change one thing {#w8-s5-4}

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Does your co-localisation survive a structure-preserving null?
observed <- cor(props[, "CD8 T"], props[, "Macrophage"])

null <- replicate(1000, {
  perm <- sample(nrow(props))          # ⚠️ a naive permutation — discuss why this is still too easy
  cor(props[perm, "CD8 T"], props[, "Macrophage"])
})

cat("observed:", round(observed, 3),
    " null 95%:", round(quantile(null, c(.025, .975)), 3), "\n")
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
# Does your co-localisation survive a structure-preserving null?
observed = np.corrcoef(props["CD8 T"], props["Macrophage"])[0, 1]

rng  = np.random.default_rng(1)
null = [np.corrcoef(rng.permutation(props["CD8 T"]),     # ⚠️ a naive permutation — discuss why this is still too easy
                    props["Macrophage"])[0, 1] for _ in range(1000)]

print("observed:", round(observed, 3), " null 95%:", np.round(np.quantile(null, [.025, .975]), 3))
```
:::


:::

⚠️ Then discuss: this permutation destroys **all** tissue structure, so it is the too-easy null from §2.2. What would a better one look like? (Hint: permute within anatomical region, or shift the whole label map rigidly.)

## 5) Before next week {#w8-s5-5}

**[W9 — proteomics](../part5/w9_proteomics_tech.qmd).** Everything so far measured RNA. Next we ask whether the protein was ever made — and find out how often the answer is no.

Nothing to install; W9 is conceptual.

# 📝 Summary

-   Deconvolution estimates the cell-type mixture of each spot using a single-cell **reference**
-   ⚠️ **The reference determines the answer.** A missing cell type is redistributed silently onto its nearest neighbour
-   ✅ Check the reference for tissue, condition, platform, and patients — then verify with an un-deconvolved marker gene
-   On single-cell platforms, **annotate** cells instead of deconvolving spots. Only panel genes count, and the label inherits the segmentation → ✅ map the confidence
-   A dominant-cell-type map hides everything that is everywhere and dominates nowhere — usually the immune compartment
-   ✅ **Niches** — clustering spots by their neighbourhood composition — is where the spatial biology lives
-   ⚠️ Complete spatial randomness is the wrong null. Permute within tissue structure, or compare to matched control tissue
-   ⚠️ Thousands of spots inflate p-values. **Effect size, replicated across patients**, is the claim
-   ✅ Compare niches with **one number per patient** (niche fraction) and a compositional test. Pooled spots = W5's per-cell test again
-   ⚠️ Spatial ligand–receptor: a distance limit removes pairs that never met, and a structure-preserving null tests the rest. Still mRNA, still rung ③
-   Spatial validation promotes a claim from *hypothesis* to *consistent with* — not to *demonstrated*
-   ✅ Design from a hypothesis, count patients not sections, select by outcome, and book the pathologist first

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 🔑 Key terms

| Term | One-line meaning |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Deconvolution | Estimating cell-type proportions within a mixed spot |
| Reference | The single-cell dataset defining what each cell type looks like |
| Reference bias | Anything absent from the reference cannot appear in the output |
| RCTD / cell2location / CARD | Common deconvolution methods |
| Absolute abundance | Estimated cell numbers rather than proportions |
| Cell-level annotation | One label per segmented cell from a single-cell reference — what replaces deconvolution on single-cell platforms |
| Panel | The genes an imaging platform measures, chosen in advance; a cell type with no marker on it cannot be called |
| Niche / neighbourhood | Recurrent local composition around a location |
| Niche fraction (per patient) | Share of a patient's section in each niche — the unit for comparing groups |
| Co-localisation | Two cell types occurring together more than expected |
| Structure-preserving null | A permutation that keeps tissue architecture intact |
| Label transfer | Projecting single-cell annotations onto spatial data |
| Spatially constrained CCC | Ligand–receptor scoring limited to cells within signalling range |
| Effective sample size | How many independent observations you really have |
| Evidence ladder | Description → hypothesis → consistent with → supported → demonstrated |
